Module 6 — Advanced Rendering · Lesson 6.17b

Local Lights: Point and Spot, and Their Shadows

Every light this engine has ever drawn is the sun: infinitely far away, arriving from one direction at one strength everywhere. A desk lamp, a torch on a wall and a car's headlight are all somewhere, and being somewhere changes two facts at once — the direction of the light varies across the scene, and its strength falls with the square of the distance. This lesson adds point and spot lights to both renderers, derives the inverse-square law from a sphere and measures it, compares the three published ways of forcing a light to zero at its range, and ramps a spot's cone in cosine. Then it gives both kinds of lamp a shadow: a perspective map for a spot and six mirrored cameras for a point. That is where the lesson stops being a port. 6.8's bias turns out to be the on-axis special case of a formula it never needed; a cube map rendered with look_at is the mirror image of the one the hardware reads; and a bug that has been in the CPU rasterizer since Module 3 — a clamp that quietly moves vertices — surfaces the first time a camera with a five-centimetre near plane looks across a floor. Every claim is judged against a ray-cast ground truth that shares no code with the engine, the two renderers agree to within one pixel of a shadow edge, and twenty-five other lessons' harnesses produce the same results they did before a line of this lesson existed.

1The problem: one light, and it is the sun

engine::lighting has held exactly one light since Lesson 3.6, and its name says what it is: directional_light. A direction of travel, a colour, and — since 6.2 — an irradiance: the power landing on each square metre of a surface held square-on to the beam. Everything Module 6 built on top of it is correct for that one kind of light. The microfacet BRDF of 6.4 does not care where the light came from; the shadow map of 6.8 was fitted to a box because the sun has no position to put a camera at; the cascades of 6.9 split the camera's frustum because the sun is the same everywhere and only the viewer's need for detail varies.

Now put a lamp on a desk. Try to fake it with what the engine has, and the failure is not subtle. A directional light pointed from the lamp toward the desk lights the desk — and it lights the floor, the far wall and the ceiling behind the lamp with the same irradiance, from the same direction, because a directional light is by definition the same everywhere. There is no pool of light. There is no falloff. The object under the lamp and the object across the room are lit identically, and the shadow of the lamp's own stand falls in parallel lines like the shadow of a building at noon. You have drawn a small sun.

What is missing is two facts, and each is a part of this lesson.

  • The direction varies. The light arrives at each surface point along the line from the lamp to that point, so l stops being a constant and becomes normalise(position − p), different at every fragment.
  • The strength falls with distance. A lamp's light spreads out as it travels, and the irradiance a surface receives falls with the square of its distance from the lamp. This is not a tuning curve; §3 derives it from the area of a sphere and then measures it.

And then the parts that are not about light at all, which are where most of the work turns out to be.

  • A scene has many lamps, and the shader must be handed all of them. Lesson 4.6 measured (and the post-Module 8 review corrected the explanation of) how SDL copies a uniform push into a 32 KiB block of which the Vulkan backend binds 4 KiB. A light list whose length the scene decides cannot live in a push. This lesson gives the fragment stage its first storage buffer.
  • A lamp needs a shadow, and 6.8's shadow was built for the sun. Its bias derivation leaned, in one place, on the camera being orthographic — every ray parallel, every texel the same size, device depth a linear function of distance. A spot light's camera is a pyramid and a point light's is six of them. §6 and §7 find out which of 6.8's results survive that, and one of them does not.

There is also something this lesson did not set out to find. It is in §8, and it is a bug that has been in the software rasterizer since Lesson 3.3 — invisible for fifty lessons because no camera in the course had ever looked the way a lamp looks.

2Building intuition: a point that pours light over spheres

Picture the lamp as a single point, pouring out power in every direction at a steady rate. Now draw a sphere around it of radius one metre. Every bit of the power the lamp emits crosses that sphere — there is nowhere else for it to go. Draw a second sphere at two metres. The same power crosses it too, but that sphere has four times the area, because a sphere's area grows with the square of its radius. The same power over four times the area is a quarter of the power per square metre. Figure 1 draws exactly this: a narrow beam of rays cuts a patch from each sphere, and the far patch has twice the width in each direction and therefore four times the area.

That is the whole of the inverse-square law, and you should notice what it is not. It is not a model of fog, or of the lamp getting tired, or of light "weakening" as it travels. Nothing is lost in empty space. The light is simply spread thinner, the way paint spread over a larger wall is a thinner coat. That framing matters, because it tells you which parts of the shading equation change. The BRDF — what a surface does with the light that reaches it — is untouched. Only the part that says how much light arrives gets a new factor.

A spot light is the same point with a hood over it. The hood blocks the light outside a cone and lets it through inside; it does not concentrate anything. Seen that way a spot light is a point light multiplied by a mask, and every result about point lights carries over with one extra factor. §5 builds the mask, and discusses the other way to see it — a hood that focuses — and why this engine, like Frostbite and like glTF's specification, chose not to.

And a shadow for either is 6.8's idea — render the scene from the light, keep the depth, compare — with a camera that is no longer a box. A spot light's camera is a pyramid down its axis. A point light sees the whole sphere, and no single camera can: six cameras with 90-degree fields of view, one per face of a cube, tile the sphere with no gap and no overlap. 6.15 built cube maps for the sky, by evaluating a function of direction into each face. This lesson is the first time the engine has to render into one, and §7 is about the one way that goes wrong that looks entirely right.

3The inverse-square law, derived and measured

3.1 — From the sphere to the formula

Call the lamp's total emitted power Φ (the radiometric "flux", in watts). If it emits equally in every direction, then a sphere of radius d centred on it — area 4πd² — receives all of it spread evenly, so the power per unit area on the sphere is

\[ E(d) = \frac{\Phi}{4\pi d^{2}} \] E(d) = Phi / (4 * pi * d^2)

That quantity — power per unit area on a surface held square-on to the light — is irradiance, the same E⊥ Lesson 6.2 gave the sun. The constant part, Φ/4π, is the power per unit solid angle leaving the lamp: its intensity I, in watts per steradian (a whole sphere of directions is 4π steradians, so dividing the total by 4π shares it out). With that name the law is

\[ E_{\perp}(d) = \frac{I}{d^{2}}, \qquad E(d) = \frac{I}{d^{2}}\,\cos\theta \] E_perp(d) = I / d^2 ; on a tilted surface, E(d) = I / d^2 * cos(theta)

and the cosine is Lesson 3.6's, unchanged: a surface tilted θ away from the direction to the lamp intercepts less of the beam, by exactly cos θ. So a local light enters the shading equation in the one place 6.2 cleared for it. Where the sun contributed E_perp · cos θ, a lamp contributes (I / d²) · cos θ, and the BRDF multiplying it is the same function.

3.2 — What the engine's intensity means

The engine stores I, not Φ, and it chooses the unit so that a lamp is directly comparable with the sun: local_light::intensity is the irradiance the lamp delivers at one metre, square-on. That is literally what I/d² means at d = 1. It inherits 6.2's exposure convention for free. The sun's default irradiance is k_reference_irradiance = π, chosen so a white Lambertian surface facing it renders at exactly 1.0; a lamp of intensity π renders that same surface at 1.0 from one metre away, and at a quarter of that from two.

Worked example. A white surface (albedo 1) faces a lamp of intensity π, and we use the pure Lambert BRDF, albedo/π, so the rendered radiance is (1/π) · E.

d = 1 m:  E = π/1  = 3.14159  →  L = 1.0000
d = 2 m:  E = π/4  = 0.78540  →  L = 0.2500
d = 4 m:  E = π/16 = 0.19635  →  L = 0.0625

verify_617b §A pushes these three through shade_local and gets 1.0000000, 0.250000 and 0.062500 — to the bit, because every factor here is exact in float. The first line is the one to hold on to: at one metre, a lamp of intensity π is the engine's sun, and the rest of the lesson can compare the two without a conversion.

glTF's KHR_lights_punctual extension specifies point and spot intensity in candela — lumens per steradian — which is I's photometric twin: the same shape of quantity, weighted by the eye's response. Its directional lights are in lux, which is E's twin. So the engine's two light types sit in exactly the relationship glTF's two do, and an importer converts both with one exposure factor (Exercise 6.17b.2).

3.3 — Measuring it rather than believing it

The derivation made one claim that can be checked directly: the same power crosses every sphere. So integrate. verify_617b §A walks spheres of radius 0.5, 2 and 8 metres on a 400×800 grid of latitude and longitude, evaluates sample_local_light at every point, and adds up irradiance × area. If the attenuation really is 1/d² every sphere collects 4πI, which for I = π is 39.47842. 

flux through a sphere around the lamp (should be 4*pi*I = 39.47842):
  r =  0.5 m   flux 39.47852   relative error 2.60e-06
  r =  2.0 m   flux 39.47852   relative error 2.60e-06
  r =  8.0 m   flux 39.47852   relative error 2.60e-06

Identical to the last digit across a sixteen-fold change in radius, and 2.6 × 10−6 from the exact value — which is the midpoint rule's own error on that grid, the same for every radius because the integrand is the same after the d² cancels. That cancellation is the law. A wrong exponent — 1/d, say, which shows up in hand-rolled lighting more often than you would think — would make the three numbers differ by factors of four.

3.4 — The singularity, and the size of a light bulb

I/d² is infinite at d = 0, and a surface can touch a lamp. The infinity is not physics: a real bulb has a size, and nothing gets inside it. The honest cure is to give the point a size, and Frostbite's course notes do exactly this: a punctual light is treated as having a physical size of one centimetre, and the squared distance is clamped below at 0.01² (Lagarde and de Rousiers 2014, §4.7 and Listing 4). The engine does the same:

\[ \text{inverse\_square}(d^{2}) = \frac{1}{\max(d^{2},\ 0.01^{2})} \] inverse_square(d_squared) = 1 / max(d_squared, 0.01^2)

Measured: at 5 mm the factor is 10,000 instead of the unclamped 40,000; at 2 cm it is 2,500, exactly 1/d². Beyond one centimetre the clamp changes nothing at all.

Unreal's answer is different and worth knowing because you will read it: Karis's 2013 notes use 1/(d² + 1) (eq. 9), which removes the singularity by changing the curve everywhere. §4 measures what that costs; the short version is that at one metre it delivers half the light the inverse square says it should.

3.5 — A far lamp is a sun, and by how much

If a point light is moved far away and its intensity scaled up by the square of the distance, it should become indistinguishable from a directional light. That is a good check of the whole construction, and it also says precisely when you may replace a distant lamp with the sun. Put the lamp D metres above the centre of a one-metre square patch, with intensity E·D². Directly beneath it the irradiance is exactly E. At a corner of the patch, r = 0.7071 m off axis, the distance is √(D² + r²) and the cosine is D/√(D² + r²), so the irradiance is E · (D/d)³ — distance and cosine together. 

   D (m)  worst deviation (D/d)^3 predicts
       2         16.1947%         16.1948%
      10          0.7453%          0.7453%
     100          0.0075%          0.0075%

The harness measures the formula exactly. The practical reading: at ten times the size of what it lights, a lamp is a sun to three-quarters of a percent, and at a hundred times, to a hundredth of that. A street light over a car park is a local light; the moon is not.

4Range: forcing zero without drawing a ring

4.1 — Why a light that never reaches zero is a problem

The inverse square never reaches zero. A lamp in the kitchen contributes a tiny, nonzero amount of light to a surface in the garage, and a shader that evaluates every lamp for every fragment will dutifully compute it. That is the cost problem: with N lamps every pixel pays N BRDF evaluations, including all the ones that add a millionth of a code. Real engines solve it by culling — deciding per tile of the screen which lamps can reach it — and culling needs every lamp to have a finite reach. So each lamp gets a range, a distance beyond which its contribution is defined to be zero. glTF's KHR_lights_punctual makes the same promise: when a light gives a range, its contribution beyond that distance is to be treated as zero.

The question is how to get from I/d² to zero at the range without the picture showing where it happened.

4.2 — Three published answers

A hard cutoff draws a visible circle on every surface a lamp reaches — a step in brightness, which the eye finds instantly. So all three published answers multiply the inverse square by a window, a function of x = d/range that is 1 near the lamp and 0 at the range:

  • glTF's recommended recipe: clamp(1 − x⁴, 0, 1) / d². The specification's README gives exactly this line.
  • Karis's window, adopted by Frostbite: saturate(1 − x⁴)² / d² — the same quartic, squared. Frostbite's notes adopt it "with value n = 4 … as presented by Karis" (eq. 26) and apply it to every punctual and area light.
  • Unreal's, from the same Karis notes: the squared window over d² + 1 instead of d², which folds the singularity cure into the curve.

The engine uses the second, with Frostbite's 1 cm clamp from §3.4 rather than Unreal's +1. Figure 2 shows why, and the next two sections measure it.

4.3 — What the window costs, and where it spends it

The fourth power keeps the window close to 1 near the lamp and spends its descent in the outer half of the range: 

       x  Karis/Frostbite    glTF recipe
   0.250         0.992203       0.996094
   0.333         0.975461       0.987654
   0.500         0.878906       0.937500
   0.700         0.577448       0.759900
   0.900         0.118267       0.343900
   0.990         0.001553       0.039404
   1.000         0.000000       0.000000

Be honest about what that means: at half its range, a lamp windowed this way delivers 12% less light than the inverse square says. That is a real change to the picture, and it is why a range is chosen generously — the window bends the part of the curve where the light is already a quarter of what it was at half the range, and dimming the dimmest part of a curve is the only place bending it is cheap. The first draft of this lesson's header comment said the window was "0.99 at half the range"; the harness says 0.879, and the comment was corrected before anything shipped.

4.4 — The edge: a crease is a ring

Why square the quartic? Look at what each window does in the last few centimetres before the range, which is the right-hand plot of Figure 2. The quantity that matters is the slope of the light just inside the edge, because the eye's edge detectors respond to a change of slope as readily as to a change of value — that is the machinery behind Mach bands, the bright and dark fringes you see beside a gradient that suddenly stops. 

dE/dd just inside the range, per unit intensity (r = 10 m):
  inverse square alone     -0.002000   (-2/r^3)
  glTF recipe              -0.004000   (-4/r^3: twice as steep, then 0)
  Karis / Frostbite        -0.000000   (0: no crease)
[PASS] glTF's edge falls 2.000x as steeply as the inverse square; the squared window's -4.8e-07

The derivation is two lines. With w(x) = 1 − x⁴, the product E = I·w/d² has derivative I·(w′/r)/d² + I·w·(−2/d³); at the range w = 0 and w′ = −4, so the slope is −4I/r³ — twice the inverse square's own slope, and then zero the instant after. That jump is a crease, and on a large floor it draws a faint ring at the range. Squaring the window makes w′ at the edge 2w·(−4x³) = 0, and the light meets zero tangentially. The harness's finite difference, taken a millimetre inside the edge, agrees: 2.000 times the inverse square's slope for glTF's recipe, and −4.8 × 10−7 — zero to within the step — for the squared window.

Note

Unreal's +1, measured as a fraction of the true inverse square: 0.20 at half a metre, 0.50 at one metre, 0.80 at two, 0.96 at five, 0.99 at ten. Karis's notes are candid that the +1 is a practical choice rather than a physical one, and suggest exposing it to artists where physical correctness is not wanted. The 1 cm clamp measures exactly 1.0000 at every one of those distances. The +1 is also a statement in metres — it assumes the world's unit is a metre — which is one more reason to prefer a clamp whose constant has a physical meaning.

5The spot: a mask, ramped in cosine

5.1 — Two angles, and what they mean

A spot light keeps everything a point light has and adds an axis — direction, the direction the light travels, the same convention directional_light pinned in capitals in Lesson 3.6 — and two half-angles measured from that axis. Inside the inner angle the lamp is at full intensity; outside the outer angle it is dark; between them it falls smoothly. These are glTF's innerConeAngle and outerConeAngle, in radians, with glTF's defaults of 0 and π/4, so a light imported with no spot block means here what it meant to the tool that exported it.

5.2 — Why cosine and not angle

The obvious ramp is linear in angle: compute the angle between the axis and the ray to the surface, and interpolate from inner to outer. It needs the angle, and a fragment does not have it — it has vectors. The dot product of the axis with the unit vector from the lamp to the surface is the cosine of that angle for the price of three multiplies, and recovering the angle would cost an acos per lamp per fragment. So the ramp is done in cosine, in the form glTF's reference code gives, with the two constants computed once per lamp on the CPU:

\[ s = \frac{1}{\max(0.001,\ \cos\theta_i - \cos\theta_o)}, \quad o = -\cos\theta_o \, s, \quad \text{cone} = \operatorname{saturate}(\cos\theta \cdot s + o)^{2} \] scale = 1 / max(0.001, cos(inner) - cos(outer)); offset = -cos(outer) * scale; cone = saturate(cos(theta) * scale + offset)^2

The max keeps a hard-edged cone (inner equal to outer) from dividing by zero; the square is the range window's trick again — the ramp reaches zero with zero slope, so the edge of the pool is soft rather than creased. glTF's reference code squares the ramp for the same reason: a falloff that drops quickly past the inner cone and then eases into darkness.

Cosine is not linear in angle, so this ramp is not the linear-in-angle one, and Figure 3 plots both. Worked through for the harness's cone (inner 0.30 rad, outer 0.45):

Worked example. The angular midpoint, 0.375 rad.

cos 0.300 = 0.955336   cos 0.450 = 0.900447   cos 0.375 = 0.930508
scale = 1 / (0.955336 − 0.900447) = 18.2185
offset = −0.900447 × 18.2185 = −16.4048
t = 0.930508 × 18.2185 − 16.4048 = 0.5477  →  t² = 0.2999

Halfway in angle, the cosine ramp has fallen to 0.2999, where the linear-in-angle ramp would give 0.25. The harness prints 0.29993. The difference is small and systematic — the cosine ramp holds its light a little longer, then falls a little faster — and it is the price of never calling acos, which is a price worth paying.

5.3 — A mask, not a lens

There is a second way to think of a spot light, and it matters because it changes what the intensity field means. Give the lamp a fixed total power Φ and let the hood focus it: all of it leaves through the cone, whose solid angle is 2π(1 − cos θo), so the intensity inside is Φ over that. Narrow the cone and the pool gets brighter. That is how a real reflector behaves, and Frostbite's notes derive it (eq. 16) before deliberately setting it aside: coupling brightness to the cone makes spot lights harder for artists to control, because narrowing a cone to light fewer pixels would also brighten them. Instead the reflector is treated as absorbing the light outside the cone, "acting like a simple masking" (eq. 17), and glTF's specification makes the same choice by defining a spot's intensity as the candela inside the cone.

The engine follows both, which is why the struct stores I directly and why §C of the harness checks that on its axis a spot light is its point light exactly — 0.109318 against 0.109318. The solid angles are still worth having in your head, because Exercise 6.17b.1 converts between the two conventions: 

 15.0 deg   0.2141 sr    1.70% of the sphere
 30.0 deg   0.8418 sr    6.70% of the sphere
 45.0 deg   1.8403 sr   14.64% of the sphere
 90.0 deg   6.2832 sr   50.00% of the sphere

glTF's default cone, 45 degrees, masks 85% of the sphere. A focusing lamp of the same power would be 6.8 times brighter inside it; a masking one is exactly as bright as the bare bulb.

6A spot's shadow: 6.8's machinery through a pyramid

Lesson 6.8 built the whole shadow-mapping apparatus — a depth-only pass from the light, a comparison against the stored depth, a bias sized from the surface's slope and the filter's reach, PCF — and every part of it was written for a camera that happened to be orthographic. Most of that was a coincidence of the sun, not a dependency. shadow_map takes a light_camera and never asks how it was built; the depth-only pass draws through whatever matrix it is handed; the comparison compares. So the plan for a spot light is the obvious one: build a perspective camera at the lamp, looking down its axis, and let everything else run. This section is about the one part of 6.8 for which that plan fails, and it opens with the failure, because the failure is the clearest statement of what a bias is for.

6.1 — The failure first

Render the two lamps of the harness scene — a warm point light on the right, a cool spot from the left, a box hovering above the ground and a thin sign standing on it — with shadows on and no bias at all. The left half of Figure 4 is the result, seen from straight above. The ground shadows itself, across both pools of light. This is the acne of 6.8, and it is here for 6.8's reason: the map stores the depth of the surface at each texel's sample point, a fragment between samples recomputes its own depth, and on a surface tilted with respect to the light half of all fragments are "downhill" of the sample they are compared with, and lose. verify_617b §F judges 67,715 points on the spot light's side and calls 19,502 of them acne — 29%. The right half is the bias this section derives: zero acne, and zero leaks, against a ground truth that shares no code with the engine.

The shape of the pattern is the tell that these are perspective maps. An orthographic map's acne is straight stripes, because its texels are the same size everywhere. Here the bulb's comes in nested squares, one family per face of its cube, and the spot's bends into arcs centred under the lamp, because a perspective map's texels grow with distance from it.

6.2 — The camera

fit_spot puts a square perspective pyramid at the lamp, looking along direction, with half-angle equal to the outer cone angle so the round pool of light is inscribed in the square map. Three decisions are worth defending.

  • The corners are wasted, deliberately. A circle inscribed in a square covers π/4 of it, so 21.5% of every spot map's texels lie outside the cone and are never read. The alternative, a circular map, does not exist; the alternative of fitting the square inside the circle would leave the edge of the pool unshadowed.
  • The near plane is 5 cm, and it cannot go far. Lesson 2.10 showed that a perspective depth buffer spends half its codes before twice the near distance, and 4.9 measured what pushing the near plane out buys. Here it cannot be pushed: anything nearer the lamp than the near plane is clipped from the shadow pass, casts nothing, and lets the light straight through. A moth on a bulb, a hand on a torch. Five centimetres is k_local_shadow_near.
  • The far plane is the range, and the cone is capped at 80°. Nothing beyond the range is lit, so nothing beyond it can matter. A spot wider than 80° from its axis is not given a spot map: its edge texels would stretch by 1/cos² 80° = 33 times, and at 90° without bound. That is a job for a cube, which is what a point light is (§7).

Figure 5 draws the pyramid and the property the rest of this section turns on. One texel of a 512 map on this spot covers 1.652 mm at one metre, 3.3 mm at two, and 13.2 mm at eight. An orthographic texel has one size; a perspective texel's size is proportional to the axial distance w of whatever it lands on. So light_camera::world_per_texel is redefined under perspective — it is the footprint at one metre — and every use of it multiplies by w first.

6.3 — 6.8's bias, carried through the depth curve

6.8 §4.4 derived the bias in three steps. The farthest filter tap is reach texels from the fragment; a texel is texel metres; walking that far across a surface tilted at θ changes its depth by that distance times tan θ. That is a bias in metres. The fourth step converted metres into the device units the comparison runs in by dividing by depth_range, the depth of the orthographic box — correct, because an orthographic projection makes device depth an affine function of distance, so one scale factor converts everywhere.

A perspective projection makes device depth a hyperbola. Written as a function of axial distance w — which is exactly what Lesson 2.10's zndc is — the engine's perspective() stores

\[ \text{depth}(w) = \frac{f\,(w - n)}{(f - n)\,w} \] depth(w) = far * (w - near) / ((far - near) * w)

— zero at the near plane, one at the far one, and steep near the lamp. There is no single scale factor. The honest conversion is also the simplest: move the point back toward the lamp by the bias in metres and ask the curve how far that moved it.

\[ \text{bias}_{\text{device}} = \text{depth}(w) - \text{depth}(w - b), \qquad b = \text{reach}\cdot(\text{texel}_{1\,\text{m}}\, w)\cdot\text{slope} \] bias_device = depth(w) - depth(w - b), where b = reach * (texel_at_1m * w) * slope

No derivative taken, nothing assumed small. Both renderers compute exactly this — the CPU in shadow_map::visibility, the GPU in local_depth_bias — with w clamped so the moved point never goes behind the near plane.

Worked example. The harness's spot: near 0.05 m, far 8 m, a 512 map. A surface at 45° on the axis, one metre out, one tap (reach ½√2 = 0.7071 texel).

texel here   = 1.652 mm × 1.0              = 1.652 mm
b           = 0.7071 × 1.652 mm × tan 45°    = 1.168 mm
depth(1.000000) = 8 × 0.950000 / (7.95 × 1.000000) = 0.9559748
depth(0.998832) = 8 × 0.948832 / (7.95 × 0.998832) = 0.9559160
bias        = 5.88 × 10−5

6.8's formula, applied unchanged, divides the same 1.168 mm by the depth range of 7.95 m and gets 1.469 × 10−4 — two and a half times too much. §F of the harness prints both across the whole range: 

   d (m)   texel mm    bias mm    derived dev  6.8 as-is dev     ratio
     0.5      0.826      0.584      1.177e-04      1.469e-04     1.248
     1.0      1.652      1.168      5.883e-05      1.469e-04     2.497
     2.0      3.303      2.336      2.939e-05      1.469e-04     4.999
     4.0      6.606      4.671      1.472e-05      1.469e-04     9.978
     8.0     13.212      9.342      7.331e-06      1.469e-04    20.036
  (6.8's formula is right at one distance only, d = near * far / 1 m = 0.40 m;
   inside it too small, outside it too large, in proportion to the distance)

Why a constant in device units goes so wrong is visible in the two curves. The texel grows like w; the depth curve's slope, fn/((f−n)w²), shrinks like 1/w²; their product — the right device bias — falls like 1/w. 6.8's constant is right exactly where those meet: at w = n·f/(1 m) = 0.40 m, the crossover the harness prints. (The "/1 m" is there because world_per_texel was defined at one metre; the first draft of that line printed "0.40 m²" and meant something dimensionally wrong.) Beyond it the constant is too large in proportion to distance. Too large is not acne — it is peter-panning, the shadow detaching from the foot of its caster — and §6.6 finds out how badly.

6.4 — The slope that an orthographic derivation cannot see

That conversion was the change this section set out to make. With it in place, the CPU and GPU renderers were compared pixel by pixel (§11 describes the instrument), and they disagreed about nineteen pixels that were nowhere near any shadow edge — five pixels and more from one, all on the ground inside the spot's pool, where the GPU's spot read slightly occluded and the CPU's read fully lit. Both were using 6.8's tan θ. A bias that is merely too small does not show up identically through two different filters, and that is how the disagreement exposed it: somewhere the slope was bigger than tan θ said.

The reason is in Figure 6, and it is the one assumption 6.8's derivation made without saying so. The map stores axial depth — the distance along the camera's axis, w — not the distance along the ray. Under an orthographic camera every ray is the axis and the two are the same number. Under perspective the rays diverge, and a wall that faces the lamp squarely, but sits off to one side of the axis, has points whose distance from the lamp is the same while their axial depth is not.

So derive the slope again, for axial depth. Put the lamp at the origin with its axis a. Lay the image plane at w = 1, and let a unit vector e in it, perpendicular to a, be the direction one texel step moves; a step of one texel moves the image point by t, the footprint at one metre. The ray through image point x along e is w·(a + xe) — every point on it at axial depth w. The receiving surface is a plane n·P = c. The ray meets it where

\[ w(x) = \frac{c}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf a + x\,\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e}, \qquad \frac{dw}{dx} = -\frac{w^{2}\,(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf e)}{c} \] w(x) = c / (n.a + x n.e); dw/dx = -w^2 (n.e) / c

and c is n·P for the point hit, which is the distance to it, dist, times the cosine between the normal and the ray: |c| = dist·cos θ. One texel is dx = t, and the worst direction e in the image plane — the one along the surface's steepest descent — makes |n·e| as large as it can be for a unit vector perpendicular to a, which is sin α, α the angle between the normal and the axis. Collecting, with w/dist = cos φ, φ the angle between the ray and the axis:

\[ \frac{\Delta w}{\text{texel}} = (t\,w)\cdot\frac{\sin\alpha\,\cos\varphi}{\cos\theta} \] axial depth change per texel = (t * w) * sin(alpha) * cos(phi) / cos(theta)

Three angles, each doing something you can name. θ (normal against ray) is the grazing term, and it diverges at the silhouette exactly as 6.8's did. α (normal against axis) is how steeply the surface cuts across the map's depth, and φ (ray against axis) is how far off-centre the texel is. On the axis φ = 0, the ray is the axis, α = θ, and the expression is tan θ — 6.8's result, recovered as the on-axis special case of this one. Off the axis they part company — on the harness's ground, lit obliquely by the spot, by enough to acne through one filter and not the other — and most sharply for a wall that faces the lamp squarely, which has θ = 0 but α = φ, and a slope of sin φ cos φ where 6.8's says zero.

Worked example. A wall facing the spot squarely, 30° off its axis, at axial distance 1 m.

tan θ                = tan 0° = 0                  (6.8: no slope bias)
sin α cos φ / cos θ = sin 30° · cos 30° / 1 = 0.4330
per texel           = 1.652 mm × 0.4330       = 0.715 mm of axial depth

Nearly half the depth change of a 45° surface, on a surface 6.8 says needs none. The fix is one function, perspective_slope, used by both renderers in place of tan θ under perspective; it cleared sixteen of the nineteen. (The last three were not a bias at all — §11 tells that story.) The normal-offset policy keeps using sin θ, correctly: it moves the point across the surface toward the lamp, and that is still about the ray.

6.5 — A slope of exactly zero, and the knife edge it exposes

The new slope does something 6.8's never did: it reaches exactly zero on a surface the light still sees. Take a point light directly above a floor and look at the floor through the cube's −Y face. The normal is +Y and the face's axis is −Y, so α = 180° and sin α = 0. That is not an approximation — every point of the floor really is the lamp's height below it, so the axial depth really is constant, and the derivation is right to ask for no geometric bias at all.

And then the comparison is on a knife edge. The pass stored the depth the rasterizer interpolated; the lookup recomputes it from the fragment's position; the two are the same real number, computed two different ways in float, and they disagree in the last bit roughly half the time. §F saw 90 points of acne appear out of nothing, in a clean square under the lamp. The cure is the term 6.8 called quantisation and set to zero for a 32-bit depth format, because an orthographic bias with the sun at an angle never reached zero to expose it: k_perspective_depth_floor, 2−22. Device depth near 1 is spaced 2−24 apart in a float; both values can be half a spacing off before they meet, and four spacings covers both with room to spare. It is 0.03 mm at 2.5 m on the harness's spot, and 90 became 0.

Why a floor and not an epsilon

"Add a tiny constant" is the folklore version of this fix, and the reason to derive it anyway is that the size is not arbitrary. Too small and the knife edge is back; too large and it is a constant bias again, with every one of §6.3's problems. The floor is sized from the float format and the depth curve near 1, where a local light's depths live — half the codes are spent before w = 0.1 m, so every surface a lamp shadows is in the part of the curve where the spacing is 2−24.

6.6 — What the judge said

Four policies, the same spot light, the same 67,715 judged points (§11 explains "judged"). The ground truth casts a ray from each point to the lamp against the analytic box, sign and ground, and shares no code with the engine. 

  spot light, 512 map        judged     acne     leak
  no bias (the acne)          67715    19502        0
  6.8's formula, as-is        67715        0       50
  derived, per fragment       67715        0        0
  normal offset               67715        0        0

The 50 leaks were harder to find than the acne, and the finding is worth recording because the prediction was refused twice first. §6.3 said 6.8's constant is too large beyond 0.4 m, so it should peter-pan: the shadow should come away from the base of whatever casts it. The first test scene put a solid half-metre crate on the ground and found no leaks. The second stood a 3 cm wall there, and again found none. Both refusals were right. An over-large bias pushes the comparison back, away from the lamp, by a distance that grows with the square of the distance and with the receiver's slope — 2.9 mm for a 45° surface one metre out, several centimetres for the floor meeting a caster at a grazing angle — and a receiver can only leak if the caster in front of it is thinner than that. Behind a solid crate, the floor lies half a metre beyond the crate's lit face along the ray, which no bias of centimetres reaches. Behind the 3 cm wall, the floor is within the bias of the lit face for about 1.3 cm — all of it inside the two-texel band around the wall's base that the judge rightly calls ambiguous (§11.2). A sign 4 mm thick leaves a predicted band of about 3.9 cm, and the third scene found 50 lit points in it where the derived bias finds none.

That is the honest size of 6.8's formula's error on a local light: it is always wrong by d/(n·f), but it is only visible through casters thinner than the over-bias. Leaves, cloth, paper, a fence of thin boards. The derived bias has no such floor on what it can shadow, and costs one call to a function both renderers already have.

7A point's shadow: six cameras and a mirror

7.1 — Six faces

A point light shines everywhere, and a perspective camera cannot see more than a hemisphere even in principle; in practice its texels stretch without bound long before that (§6.2's 1/cos²). The standard answer, and the one the hardware is built for, is a cube map: six square 90° cameras, one down each axis, whose pyramids tile the sphere around the lamp with no gap and no overlap. Lesson 6.15 built cube maps for the sky, by evaluating a function of direction into each face texel. The table that says which direction lands on which texel of which face was written there, once, as k_rules in cubemap.cpp, and verified against the hardware's own lookup: 

{ 2, 1, 0, -1.0f, -1.0f },   // +X : sc = -z, tc = -y
{ 2, 1, 0, +1.0f, -1.0f },   // -X : sc = +z, tc = -y
{ 0, 2, 1, +1.0f, +1.0f },   // +Y : sc = +x, tc = +z
{ 0, 2, 1, +1.0f, -1.0f },   // -Y : sc = +x, tc = -z
{ 0, 1, 2, +1.0f, -1.0f },   // +Z : sc = +x, tc = -y
{ 0, 1, 2, -1.0f, -1.0f },   // -Z : sc = -x, tc = -y

This lesson renders into a cube for the first time, and so needs the same table in the other direction: for each face, which camera draws an image that lands on that face the way the lookup reads it. cube_face_axes turns each row into three vectors — the face's u (the direction that increases the horizontal texture coordinate), v (the vertical one, which grows down the image) and major (the axis the face looks along) — derived from k_rules itself, so the two directions of the table can never disagree. SDL orders the faces +X, −X, +Y, −Y, +Z, −Z, so face f of cube c in an array is layer 6c + f.

7.2 — The camera that is a mirror

The obvious camera for the +X face is look_at(lamp, lamp + (1,0,0), up) with some sensible up vector, and it is wrong in a way that looks right. Work it through with one direction.

Worked example. The direction d = (1, 0.2, −0.5) from the lamp. Its largest component is x, so the hardware reads it from the +X face.

the lookup (k_rules, +X): sc = −z = 0.5, tc = −y = −0.2, ma = 1
texture coordinates          : u = (0.5 + 1)/2 = 0.75, v = (−0.2 + 1)/2 = 0.40

fit_cube_face, rows (u, −v, −major) = ((0,0,−1), (0,1,0), (−1,0,0)):
view space                   : (0.5, 0.2, −1)  → ndc (0.5, 0.2)
viewport, y down             : x = 0.75, y = (1 − 0.2)/2 = 0.40  ✓

look_at's right-hand frame, rows (−u, −v, −major):
view space                   : (−0.5, 0.2, −1) → x = 0.25  ✗ (half a face away)

The two frames differ in the sign of one row. The face's (u, v, major) with v flipped for the image is a left-handed frame — its determinant is −1 — and no rotation, which is all look_at can build, has determinant −1. So the correct camera for a cube face is a reflection, and fit_cube_face builds it from the rows directly.

This is the trap that looks entirely right, and it is worth being precise about why. A mirrored face still contains the scene's depth, drawn from the right place, in the right direction, at the right resolution. Rendered to the screen, each face looks like a perfectly good picture. The error only shows as shadows that land on the wrong side of their casters, mirrored about each face's centre line — which in a busy scene looks like "the shadows are a bit off", not "the image is flipped". §E of the harness measures both frames on all six faces, 1,089 directions each: 

   face  det(ours)  det(look_at)   worst uv err   look_at err
     +X    -1.0000        1.0000       1.19e-07        0.9697
     -X    -1.0000        1.0000       1.64e-07        0.9697
     +Y    -1.0000        1.0000       1.64e-07        0.9697
     -Y    -1.0000        1.0000       1.34e-07        0.9697
     +Z    -1.0000        1.0000       1.34e-07        0.9697
     -Z    -1.0000        1.0000       1.79e-07        0.9697

The mirror lands every direction on the texel the lookup reads, to 1.8 × 10−7 of a face — rounding. look_at misses by up to 0.97 of a face on every one of them. (The mirror reverses triangle winding too. Both shadow passes cull nothing by default, so they do not care — but 6.8's third acne cure, culling front faces, would cull the wrong faces on a cube, and §15 lists it as a pitfall.)

7.3 — Reading it back with no matrix at all

A spot's lookup projects the fragment through the map's clip_from_world, as 6.8's did. A point light's needs none, and this is the elegant part. The hardware picks the face from the direction's largest component; that same component is the distance along the face's axis — w in the face camera's clip space — so the depth the pass stored for this direction is perspective_depth(max(|dx|, |dy|, |dz|), near, far), predicted from the direction alone. The shader passes the direction and the reference depth to one SampleCmpLevelZero on a TextureCubeArray; the CPU asks direction_to_cube for the face and texel, and runs the ordinary map lookup on that face. §E checks the claim: the stored depth is perspective_depth(major axis) to 1.8 × 10−7.

7.4 — The seams

A direction exactly on the 45° seam between two faces has two largest components. The lookup picks one; the other face's camera also contains it, on its edge. With float rounding, a point the lookup assigns to face A can project a hair past −1 on face A's own camera. 6.8's orthographic lookup rejects anything outside [−1, 1] as "not in this map, so lit" — the right answer for a box fitted around the scene, and the wrong one here, where the face was chosen because it owns this direction. The CPU found 54 points on the seams leaking light through a crate's shadow before the rule changed. Under perspective the lookup now clamps to the face instead of rejecting (for a spot the clamp can only touch points outside the fitted square, where the cone is already zero), and §E closes the argument from the other side: of 20,000 random directions, 0 fall outside the frustum of the face that owns them.

7.5 — What a cube costs

A 256² cube is six 256² faces: 393,216 texels against a 512² spot map's 262,144, 1.5 times the texels and six render passes to one. The defaults — 512 for a spot, 256 for a cube face — are a budget, not a law, and they buy different sharpness: a cube face spreads 90° over 256 texels, 7.8 mm per texel at one metre, while a spot with glTF's default 45° cone spreads the same 90° over 512, 3.9 mm. A default point light's shadow is exactly twice as coarse as a default spot's, for 1.5 times the memory. On the CPU, in a release build, the harness's spot map takes 0.72 ms and its six-face cube 0.35 ms, which says the cost is covered texels, not passes: most of a point light's six faces see only a little of the scene. On the GPU, gpu_local_shadows gives each kind its own budget — four spots and two points by default, as a depth Texture2DArray and a depth TextureCubeArray — and a shadowed lamp past its budget is drawn unshadowed with a warning, not dropped (§J: one dropped, slot −1).

⚠ VERIFY discharged

Whether SDL_GPU offers a depth cube array on every backend was not assumed. create_depth_cube_array asks SDL_GPUTextureSupportsFormat with SDL_GPU_TEXTURETYPE_CUBE_ARRAY first and logs a refusal. Read at the SDL release-3.4.12 tag: Metal's texture creation is type-agnostic for depth formats, Vulkan's queries CUBE_COMPATIBLE support per format, and D3D12's creates TEXTURECUBEARRAY views of depth resources; each backend builds a per-layer depth-stencil view, so rendering into one face of one cube is a normal render pass with layer_or_depth_plane set. The harness ran on Metal. ⚠ VERIFY on your platform: that the capability query returns true on your GPU — the engine will say so in the log if it does not.

8A Module 3 bug, found by a lamp

With the bias of §6 derived and the cube of §7 built, the CPU renderer's spot light still had acne on 88% of the floor, and no amount of bias removed it. The map was checked directly: at a point where the floor sat at device depth 0.987, the map held 0.950. Not a bias problem. The map itself was wrong.

The cause had been in the software rasterizer since Lesson 3.3, and it is a lesson in the difference between finite and small. Near-plane clipping bounds the perspective divide: every vertex that survives has w ≥ near, so x/w is finite. But a vertex on the near plane sits near metres in front of the camera and may sit metres to the side, and its screen coordinate is that sideways distance over near, times the focal length, times half the width of the target. A player camera 1.7 m above a floor with a 0.1 m near plane keeps that within a few thousand pixels, which is why nothing in Modules 3–6 ever noticed. A lamp's camera has a 5 cm near plane over an 8 m floor, and its clipped corners project to about 40,000 pixels.

to_pixel clamps every coordinate to ±8,000, and it was written for a good reason: under near_mode::none — Lesson 3.3's "watch it break" mode — coordinates can be anything, and the clamp keeps the float-to-integer conversion and edge_function's products defined. Under near_mode::clip it was never supposed to fire. When it does, it moves the vertex. The triangle changes shape; the plane of depths across it tilts; every depth interpolated inside the 512-pixel map is wrong, by an amount that depends on how far the corner was dragged. Figure 8 draws it.

The fix is the one GPUs use, and it is the reason hardware has a guard band at all. Clip against four more planes, placed where the rasterizer's integers stop being exact, so nothing reaching the rasterizer can land outside that range. A clipped vertex is placed on the true edge, by the same interpolation 3.3's near clip uses, so the plane of depths is untouched. The planes are derived in clip space from the viewport map: screen x = vp.x + vp.w(x/w + 1)/2 stays below the band exactly when x/w ≤ hx, and multiplying through by w — positive, because the near clip ran first — gives the plane hxw − x ≥ 0. The band sits at ±7,936 rather than 8,000, leaving 64 pixels for the rounding of a vertex that lands exactly on a guard plane, so the clamp can never fire on geometry that went through the guard clip.

Two properties make the fix safe to put under fifty lessons of pictures.

  • It runs only when it must. outside_guard_band checks the near-clipped polygon first; a triangle that never touched the band takes exactly the path it always took, bit for bit. clip_stats::guard_clipped counts the ones that did.
  • The reference render proves it. §D compares the eight-frame golden render byte for byte: 1,382,416 bytes, 0 differing, E917C06C. No frame in Modules 3 to 6 ever reached the band, so none of them changes; and the harnesses of every later lesson agree (§11).

The polygon bound follows the same argument as 3.3's: a triangle is three vertices, each plane can add at most one, and there are five planes in total — the near plane's one extra (3.3's k_clip_max_vertices = 4) and four guards' — so k_guard_max_vertices is 8.

9Two renderers, two filters, one reach

6.8 sized the bias from the filter's reach: how far, in texels, the farthest sample the filter reads can be from the point being shaded. With the lamps in place, the two renderers turned out to need different reaches for different reasons — and to end at the same number.

9.1 — The GPU reads four texels

The CPU's lookup compares against the nearest texel, whose sample is at most half a texel away along each axis: a reach of (r + ½)√2 for a PCF radius r, 6.8's pcf_reach_texels. The GPU's one tap is SampleCmpLevelZero through a linear comparison sampler, which compares four texels and blends the results — hardware 2×2 PCF — and any of those four can carry weight while a whole texel away along each axis. Sized for the CPU's reach, the GPU showed acne across both pools: 11,098 pixels on which the renderers disagreed, none near a shadow edge. With (r + 1)√2, zero.

Which raises an uncomfortable question about the sun. 6.8's GPU path samples through the same kind of sampler and sizes its bias with the CPU's pcf_reach_texels — with its default 3×3 kernel, 2.12 texel diagonals where 2.83 are reachable, a quarter short. This lesson does not change it: the sun's picture is not this lesson's to move, and every later lesson's harness would move with it. It is recorded in STATE.md as a pending correction, with the number to check, for the lesson that next has reason to measure the sun's shadow on the GPU.

9.2 — The CPU snaps its vertices

Then a bare floor under a bulb, with nothing at all to cast a shadow, came out striped along one cube face on the CPU — Figure 9, 713 points of acne out of 128,122. Nothing casts there; every dark mark is the map disagreeing with itself. The cause is Lesson 2.2's integer edge functions: the rasterizer snaps every vertex to a whole pixel before it fills. Snapping moves a triangle's corners by up to half a pixel, and so slides its plane of depths sideways by up to half a texel's worth of slope. A small triangle barely notices. A floor clipped to the guard band is thousands of pixels across, and a sub-pixel shift at a corner 7,936 pixels away is a real tilt across the map. The harness measured a stored depth 0.36 of a texel's depth step nearer than the analytic floor — 1.19 × 10−4 in device units.

So the CPU's perspective reach grows by half a texel diagonal, 0.7071: half a texel from the nearest sample, half from the snap, (r + 1)√2. 713 became 0; in gltf_view's scene, 1,895 became 0. The 713 is measured by running the same code with its slope scale halved, which is exactly 6.8's reach again (½√2 of a texel instead of √2), so the only thing that differs between the two panels of Figure 9 is the half texel — and the zero is evidence that the reach did it rather than that the floor stopped being tested.

The two renderers now apply the same reach for two different reasons, and both comments say which reason is theirs. That matters for the next person to touch either: "the GPU and CPU have the same constant" invites someone to share it, and the day the GPU gets a nearest-texel sampler or the CPU gets sub-pixel precision, a shared constant would be wrong for one of them without anything changing in the file that defines it.

10Implementation

Twenty-two files change and none is created, which is itself a design statement: a local light is a new kind of term in sums the engine already computes, a new kind of camera for machinery it already has, and a new kind of resource in a shader interface it already binds. The order below is the order the work was done in and the order a student should type it: the CPU renderer first, completely, because the CPU renderer is the one you can step through; then the GPU, held to it pixel by pixel.

10.1 — The light, and a function lifted out of shade()

light.hpp gains the struct and the four factors of §3–§5, each a few lines, each named for what it is: 

struct local_light
{
    local_light_kind kind = local_light_kind::point;

    vec3 position{0.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f};
    vec3 direction{0.0f, -1.0f, 0.0f};   ///< spot axis, direction of TRAVEL, unit length

    linear_rgb colour{1.0f, 1.0f, 1.0f}; ///< in linear light, as the sun's is
    float intensity = k_reference_irradiance;   ///< irradiance at 1 m, square-on

    float range = 10.0f;

    float inner_angle = 0.0f;                   ///< spot only, radians from the axis
    float outer_angle = 0.78539816f;            ///< spot only, radians; pi/4

    bool casts_shadow = false;
};

Every default is someone else's default on purpose: the intensity is the sun's, so a default-constructed lamp is comparable with the light the student already has; the cone is glTF's, so an imported spot with no cone block means what its exporter meant; and casts_shadow is off, because a shadow costs a render pass (six, for a point) and should be asked for.

range_window takes the squared distance and never calls sqrt: (d/r)⁴ is (d²/r²)², and d² is what dot(d, d) produced anyway. A range of zero or less means infinite, which returns 1 and lets §A measure the bare inverse square. 

[[nodiscard]] inline local_light_sample sample_local_light(const local_light& light,
                                                           vec3 surface_pos)
{
    local_light_sample s;
    const vec3 d = light.position - surface_pos;
    s.distance_sq = dot(d, d);
    s.to_light = normalised_or(d, vec3{0.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f});

    s.attenuation = inverse_square(s.distance_sq) * range_window(s.distance_sq, light.range);
    if (light.kind == local_light_kind::spot)
    {
        s.attenuation *= spot_cone(dot(light.direction, -s.to_light), cone_terms_of(light));
    }
    return s;
}

sample_local_light is split from the shading because the shadow lookup needs the same direction and distance, and computing them twice is how a shadow and the light it belongs to end up disagreeing about where the lamp is. shade_local then does what shade() does for the sun, with the arriving irradiance replaced: colour × intensity × attenuation × cos θ × visibility, times the BRDF.

And the BRDF is the same one, not a copy. shade()'s dispatch — Lambert, Blinn-Phong or Cook–Torrance, with the NDF choice — is lifted into surface_brdf() statement for statement, and both call it. The words "statement for statement" carry the proof obligation: a lift that reordered one multiplication would change a float somewhere in the reference render, and §D checks that it did not — 1,382,416 bytes, 0 differing. A lamp a kilometre out, scaled to deliver the sun's irradiance, then agrees with the sun to 2.84 × 10−5 over 2,310 evaluations, which is the same comparison from the other side: one BRDF, two ways of delivering light to it. (Why 2.84 × 10−5 and not zero: with coordinates of a thousand metres the direction to the lamp differs from the sun's in the last bits of a float, and a GGX lobe at roughness 0.2 turns a 10−7 change in n·h into a relative change hundreds of times larger. The bound is on the rounding, 10−4, and the harness says why.)

10.2 — The CPU renderer: a loop after shade()

fill_style gains two members — local_lights, a std::span<const local_light>, and local_shadows, a pointer that may be null — and the fragment path in raster.cpp gains one loop, after shade() and before 6.15's ambient term: 

if (!style.local_lights.empty())
{
    const vec3 gn = normalised_or(n, vec3{0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f});
    for (std::size_t k = 0; k < style.local_lights.size(); ++k)
    {
        const local_light& lamp = style.local_lights[k];
        const local_light_sample at = sample_local_light(lamp, p);
        if (at.attenuation <= 0.0f) { continue; }

        float lamp_visibility = 1.0f;
        if (style.local_shadows != nullptr && lamp.casts_shadow)
        {
            lamp_visibility = style.local_shadows->visibility(
                k, p, gn, dot(gn, at.to_light));
        }

        const linear_rgb c = shade_local(albedo, p, shading_normal, style.eye - p,
                                         lamp, style.surface, style.model,
                                         ndf_model::ggx, lamp_visibility);
        direct = {direct.r + c.r, direct.g + c.g, direct.b + c.b};
    }
}

Three decisions are in those lines. The loop sits after shade(), not inside it, because light is additive (conventions §7c) — a second source is a second term in the sum and nothing about the first changes, so an empty span leaves direct untouched to the bit. The early out comes before the shadow lookup, because the lookup is the expensive part and pointless for a pixel outside the lamp's reach. And the shadow's cosine is taken against the geometric normal and this lamp's own direction: 6.8's rule, one cosine per light. A span is the right type for a list the renderer only reads and the caller owns — the style guide's rule for non-owning access — and it is what makes "no lamps" the default with no special case.

10.3 — The CPU shadows: two fitters and a set

light_camera learns it can be perspective: a flag (false by default, so every camera built before this lesson is unchanged), the near and far planes (the depth curve needs them), and the eye and axis (the slope of §6.4 needs them). fit_spot and fit_cube_face produce such cameras. The cube face's view is built from rows, which is the one line in the lesson worth reading twice: 

const cube_axes ax = cube_face_axes(face);
const vec3 r = ax.u;
const vec3 upv = -ax.v;
const vec3 back = -ax.major;
const vec3 p = light.position;

// Column-major storage (conventions §3): each braced group is a COLUMN.
cam.view_from_world = mat4{
    {r.x, upv.x, back.x, 0.0f},
    {r.y, upv.y, back.y, 0.0f},
    {r.z, upv.z, back.z, 0.0f},
    {-dot(r, p), -dot(upv, p), -dot(back, p), 1.0f}};

A view matrix's rows are the camera's right, up and back axes — Lesson 2.9's definition, which look_at builds from a forward and an up hint. Here all three are dictated by the face table rather than chosen. look_at(p, p + major, −v) would compute the same up and back and then derive right as forward × up, which for every face is −u. Writing the rows out is the whole fix.

local_shadow_set then owns one shadow_map per shadowed spot and six per shadowed point — built on 6.8's shadow_map, not beside it. The rasterizer, the depth format, the PCF loop and the bias policies are all 6.8's; what 6.17b adds to shadow_map::visibility is the perspective branch of §6 (texel × w, the new slope, the depth curve, the rounding floor, the clamp at the face) and nothing else. The orthographic path computes nothing new and is bit-identical, which the golden and every later harness confirm. The set's own visibility picks the map: a spot's is its own; a point's is the face direction_to_cube(p − position) says owns the direction.

10.4 — The guard band, in the one place it belongs

clip.hpp gains §8's four planes, the test and the clipper; soft_renderer.cpp computes the planes once per call from the viewport and uses them in exactly one case — near_mode::clip, on a polygon outside_guard_band says has left the band — fanning the result into triangles from the same vertex the near clip fans from. Every other triangle takes the path it took yesterday.

10.5 — To the GPU: one record per lamp, in a storage buffer

6.15 left one float of padding at offset 180 of the fragment light block. It becomes local_light_count, guarded by a static_assert that says why it matters: the count lands in the pad, or it is not free. Everything else about a lamp goes in a record the fragment stage reads from a storage buffer, the first the engine has bound to a fragment shader:

Why not push the lamps as uniforms, like everything else so far? Lesson 4.6 measured the answer without knowing it was one: SDL takes every uniform push from a 32 KiB block, and the Vulkan backend's descriptor covers only 4 KiB of each. At 176 bytes a lamp, that is 23 lamps before one backend silently reads past the end — a ceiling set by an implementation detail of a single backend, on a list whose length the scene decides. A storage buffer (SDL_GPU_BUFFERUSAGE_GRAPHICS_STORAGE_READ) is bound rather than pushed, so its bytes move once per frame instead of once per draw, and its size is whatever the scene needs.

Two rules keep the record's layout honest across three compilers. Every member is a float4, so DXC, glslang and SPIRV-Cross have nothing to disagree about — StructuredBuffer packing rules for mixed scalar and vector members are exactly where they do. And the matrix is stored as four rows, not as a float4x4, so no default matrix packing can transpose it on the way; the shader takes four dot products. Three static_asserts pin the size (176) and two offsets.

10.6 — The resource layout, and two numbers that disagree on purpose

The fragment shader now declares eight sampled textures and one storage buffer: 

Texture2DArray<float>   spot_shadows  : register(t6, space2);
SamplerComparisonState  spot_shadow_cmp  : register(s6, space2);
TextureCubeArray<float> point_shadows : register(t7, space2);
SamplerComparisonState  point_shadow_cmp : register(s7, space2);

StructuredBuffer<LocalLight> local_lights : register(t8, space2);

and the C++ binds the storage buffer at slot 0. The shader says t8; the renderer says 0. Both are right. SDL_GPU numbers each resource kind from zero on the C++ side — sampler slot 0, storage-buffer slot 0 — while its HLSL resource layout (the comment block above SDL_CreateGPUShader in SDL_gpu.h) puts sampled textures, then storage textures, then storage buffers into one t sequence in space 2. Eight sampled textures occupy t0–t7, so the first storage buffer is t8. On Metal the translated shader shows the same thing from a third angle: the buffer lands at [[buffer(3)]], after the three uniform blocks, and the cube array becomes depthcube_array<float>. The comment at the bind says all of this, because the next person to add a sampled texture moves the storage buffer to t9 and must know that slot 0 does not change.

10.7 — gpu_local_shadows: budgets, jobs, and a shared depth pass

gpu_shadow.cpp already built a depth-only pipeline and recorded depth draws for the sun's cascades. Those two pieces move into an anonymous namespace — build_depth_only_pipeline, record_depth_draws, begin_depth_pass — with every log string and debug event kept identical, so 6.8's and 6.9's harness transcripts do not move. The new class uses them for lamps:

  • create makes one depth Texture2DArray of max_spots layers and one depth TextureCubeArray of max_points cubes — the latter through gpu_texture::create_depth_cube_array, which asks SDL_GPUTextureSupportsFormat first (§7.5).
  • prepare(lights, out) packs one gpu_local_light per lamp, assigns shadow slots in list order within each kind's budget, and emits a job per pass to record: one for a spot, six for a point. A shadowed lamp past its budget keeps slot −1 and is drawn unshadowed, with a warning naming the budget.
  • render records every job as its own render pass; render_into records one job into a pass somebody else began — the frame graph's shape, which §10.9 uses.

A point light's record carries no matrix, and §7.3 is why: the cube lookup takes a direction and the depth is the major axis. Its four rows stay zero.

10.8 — gpu_scene: the caller's list, the renderer's count

render and render_batched take one more trailing argument, a const scene_local_lights* defaulting to null, so every existing caller compiles and behaves as before. The struct holds the light buffer, its count, the two shadow textures and the comparison sampler. Three things happen with it.

  • The count is the renderer's, not the caller's. The count the shader loops to and the buffer it indexes must describe the same list, and the only place both are in hand is begin_frame. So the light block is pushed from a copy whose local_light_count the renderer sets — zero unless a real list arrived. A caller cannot make the shader read past the end of a buffer by leaving a stale number in a struct.
  • Every declared resource is bound, always. A shader that declares a storage buffer must have one bound even if its loop runs zero times — SDL's debug layer asserts "Missing fragment storage buffer binding" at draw time. The renderer owns three identity elements for the case where the caller has no lamps or no shadows: a zeroed one-record light buffer, a one-layer depth array and a one-cube depth cube array, both cleared to the far plane at creation (seven empty render passes, once). 6.15 established the pattern for its environment maps; the caller never has to know the shader has these slots. And they are created with the types their slots declare, which 6.8's own fallback for the sun's slot turned out not to be: it was a plain 2D texture in the slot 6.9 re-declared Texture2DArray. It rendered correctly, and Metal's validation layer (MTL_DEBUG_LAYER=1) reported it on every draw that used it — twelve times in this lesson's harness. The first version of this page said Metal tolerated it and set it as an exercise; run under the validation layer, it did not, and it is now a one-layer array like the other two.
  • The frame-constant samplers are bound together, now eight of them, in bind_fragment_samplers, and the storage buffer at slot 0 in bind_local_lights, which records a bind_storage event in 4.9's frame log, so a dump of the frame shows the binding.
A correction carried here

Until this lesson, the comment in gpu_scene.cpp explained binding all the samplers in one call by saying a partial SDL_BindGPUFragmentSamplers "replaces the range it names", unbinding everything outside it. The post-Module 8 review read SDL's source at release-3.4.12 and found otherwise: all three backends write only firstSlot + i, and what resets bindings is ending the pass. The measurement behind the old comment was right and its explanation wrong. This lesson rewrites the function anyway, so it carries the correction: binding all eight together is still correct and still one call — only the reason changed. Exercise 6.17b.3 cashes in what the corrected rule permits.

10.9 — The frame graph: seven passes declared, and a frame that declares none

6.17 built the frame graph for passes like these, and a lamp's shadow is the first new pass to arrive since. Each job becomes one declared pass with one statement: it clears one layer of an imported texture. The scene pass samples both textures. 

engine::fg_texture spots  = fg.import("spot shadows",  shadows.spot_texture(),  spot_desc);
engine::fg_texture points = fg.import("point shadows", shadows.point_texture(), point_desc);

for (int j = 0; j < shadows.job_count(); ++j)
{
    const engine::local_shadow_job& job = shadows.job(j);
    const int p = fg.add_pass(names[j], &exec_local, &ctx[j]);
    if (job.kind == local_light_kind::spot) { spots  = fg.clear_depth(p, spots,  1.0f, job.layer); }
    else                                    { points = fg.clear_depth(p, points, 1.0f, job.layer); }
}

const int scene = fg.add_pass("scene", &exec_scene, &sctx);
fg.sample(scene, spots);
fg.sample(scene, points);

6.17's rules then derive everything. A clear of one layer keeps the other layers, so it consumes the previous version and produces the next: the six faces form a chain, and because the scene samples the chain's last version, every face's store op comes out STORE. §I prints the derived ops — seven CLEAR/STORE shadow passes, the scene's colour CLEAR/STORE and its depth CLEAR/DONT_CARE, 4.7's choice derived again — and the declared frame matches the hand-recorded one on all 196,608 channels.

The second frame in Figure 11 is the one to notice. Shadows of static lamps over static geometry do not change between frames, and the graph already knows how to express "use what is there": an import's version 0 is real — it is whatever the texture holds when the frame begins. A frame that declares no shadow passes samples version 0 of both imports, and the graph runs one pass. §I: 0 channels differ from the frame that rendered the maps, and the control — clear the maps first, then run the cached frame — changes 18,015. Deciding when a cached map is stale (a lamp moved, a caster moved into its range) is an engine policy this lesson does not write; the graph's part, making the cached frame expressible and correct, is done.

10.10 — The shader loop

scene.frag.hlsl gets the same lift as light.hpp — surface_brdf and specular_alpha move out of main so the sun and the lamps share them — and then one line in main: 

float3 lit = f_r * e + ambient_term;
if (local_light_count > 0.5f)
{
    lit += shade_local_lights(p, n, geometric, v, base, diffuse_albedo, spec_f0, ct_alpha);
}

shade_local_lights is raster.cpp's loop in HLSL, in the same order — where the lamp is, an early out, then the shadow, then the BRDF — because §G holds the two renderers to one another pixel by pixel, and the easiest way to make two implementations agree is to make them the same sequence of operations. The guard on the count is not an optimisation: with no lamps the loop body is never reached and the sun's pixels are bit-for-bit what they were, which §H checks.

10.11 — The demo

gltf_view --lights puts two lamps into the CPU renderer's scene, sized from the model's bounds so any model works: a warm bulb to one side at half the model's span above the floor, and a cool spot high on the other side, aimed at the floor beside the model. Each is given the intensity that delivers twice the sun's reference irradiance where it is aimed — 2π · d² for a lamp d metres from that point, §3.2's unit doing its job — and the sun is turned down to a tenth, so the lamps dominate and the picture reads as night with a lamp on. --lamp-shadows 0 drops both maps.

11The instruments, and the judge that was wrong four times

verify_617b runs forty checks in ten sections, and each section's shape is 5.3's rule: a measurement, a claim, and a control that proves the measurement could have failed. Three instruments carry most of the lesson, and each has a story about being wrong.

11.1 — Two renderers held to each other

§G renders one lit ground from straight above through both renderers, with the same two lamps, and compares every pixel in linear light. Each pixel is a known floor point, so a disagreement has a location, and every disagreement is classified by its distance to the nearest shadow edge in the CPU's image. Without shadows the renderers agree on all 62,940 lit pixels to 2 × 10−4 relative, worst 1.66 × 10−5. With them: 

  with shadows: 61043 lit pixels, 60784 agree, 259 differ; 6115 shadowed lamp-pixels
  disagreeing pixels by distance to the nearest CPU shadow edge:
    <=1 px 259   <=2 px 0   <=3 px 0   <=4 px 0   <=5 px 0   beyond 0

Every one of the 259 is within a pixel of a shadow edge, where the two filters legitimately differ — nearest-texel on one side, a 2×2 bilinear comparison on the other — and they are 259 of the 4,340 pixels in that band. The control widens the spot's cone by 5% and moves 9,992 pixels, so an instrument that reports 259 can see ten thousand. This comparison is what found the GPU's reach (§9.1, 11,098 disagreements off any edge) and the perspective slope (§6.4, nineteen). The last three of those nineteen were not a bias at all: they sat on the rim of the spot's cone, where the attenuation is a few parts in 105 and the two renderers' rounding of spot_cone differed by more than the relative tolerance. The comparison gained an absolute floor of 10−5 — nearly four hundred times smaller than one step of an 8-bit display — and the harness says why next to it.

11.2 — A judge that shares no code with the engine

§F's acne and leak counts need to know, at each point, whether the lamp really sees it. The judge answers by casting a ray from the point to the lamp against the analytic box, sign and ground — no shadow map, no rasterizer, no engine geometry. Then it has to decide which points it is allowed to judge, because a point exactly at a shadow's edge has no right answer at a map's resolution: the map cannot resolve anything finer than a texel, so both answers are defensible there. Excluding those ambiguous points is correct. Deciding which they are was wrong four times.

  1. A fixed 6 cm on the floor around each shadow's edge. A texel's shadow at grazing incidence is wider than that.
  2. One and a half texels on the floor. Scaled with the map, and still too narrow.
  3. Two texels on the floor. It failed on a point whose ray clears the top edge of the box by a fifth of a texel and then travels another three metres to the ground. No floor position within half a metre of that point is anywhere near the box's shadow — and yet the map, which resolves directions from the lamp one texel apart, cannot tell whether that ray grazed the box or not. The ambiguity was never on the floor. It was in the angle.
  4. Two texels of angle, tested only at the two ends. The ray was tilted two texels' worth each way, and stepped straight over the 4 mm sign, which is half a texel wide — the very aliasing the map itself suffers from.

The judge that shipped measures ambiguity in the light's own angles, densely: it tilts the ray from the lamp by every quarter of a texel's angular size, out to two texels, in two perpendicular directions each way, re-places the point along each tilted ray at its own distance, and calls it ambiguous if any tilt changes the answer. That is the resolution the map actually has, expressed in the only coordinates where it is the same everywhere. With it, the derived bias scores 0 acne and 0 leaks over 67,715 spot points and 343,360 cube points — and the controls (no bias: 19,502 and 119,886 acne) show the same judge can see failure in both.

The four wrong judges are recorded in the harness, above the one that replaced them, because the pattern will recur. Each was caught the same way: by probing a single flagged point until it explained itself — rather than excusing it, and rather than changing the engine until the count went to zero. A judge that flags a point is making a claim about the engine and about itself, and the question to ask first is whether it is measuring in the coordinates the thing it judges actually has.

11.3 — Twenty-nine harnesses that must not move

An inserted lesson has an obligation an appended one does not: the lessons after it were written first, and their measurements must survive it. scratch/_base617b/run_all.sh reruns the harnesses of 6.1 through 6.18 and 7.1 through 7.8 on the engine before and after this lesson, and classify.py diffs the transcripts, masking only lines that carry a unit of time. Twenty-five of the twenty-six build at HEAD — two of them only through a one-line include shim, because 8.4 moved bounds.hpp — and 6.8's does not build at HEAD at all, for a reason older than this lesson. What differs is timing lines, ratios computed from timings, and one printed heap pointer; nothing else. (6.5's harness reports the same two failures before and after — also older than this lesson, and recorded as such.) The golden render is byte-identical. That is the evidence behind "additive", and it is why the guard band could go under fifty lessons of pictures.

12The ninety-percent picture

This is the ninety-percent picture of local lights. The missing ten percent, named so nobody mistakes the silence for a claim:

  • Every lamp is evaluated for every fragment. The range makes a lamp's reach finite, which is the precondition for culling, but nothing culls yet. Real engines bin lamps into screen tiles or clusters (a compute pass per frame) and loop only over each pixel's own list — Olsson, Billeter and Assarsson's clustered shading (2012), and the tiled and clustered forward shading of RTR4 chapter 20. 6.18b's compute shaders are the tool; the scale at which it pays is dozens of lamps, not two.
  • Lamps are points. A real bulb has a size, which softens its highlights and its shadows. The 1 cm clamp is the only acknowledgement of size here. Area lights — spheres, tubes, rectangles — are the rest of Frostbite 2014's lighting chapter and the subject of Karis 2013's representative-point trick, and their shadows need penumbra estimation (PCSS). The GGX highlight of a point light on a very smooth surface is therefore a pinprick that aliases; 6.14's specular antialiasing reduces it and does not cure it.
  • The cube's PCF stops at the face edge on the CPU. The GPU's one tap is 2×2 PCF and blends across face edges in hardware; the CPU's six maps cannot, so point lights default to radius 0 on both renderers for parity. Exercise 6.17b.4 widens it.
  • Shadow budgets are fixed at creation (four spots, two points), and a shadowed lamp past its budget goes unshadowed. Choosing which lamps get shadows each frame — by screen size, distance, importance — is a policy real engines spend real effort on, and the budget-and-warning here is only its mechanism.
  • Cached shadows need an invalidation policy (§10.9). The graph can express a cached frame; deciding when a lamp's map is stale is not written.
  • Lamps have no volumetric scattering and no IES profiles. Real luminaires emit anisotropically, described by photometric profiles; the cone is a first approximation of one.
